it is pretty concerning that a lot of level headed people are moving the discussion away from model capabilities and dismissing the hugging face incident as just human error and silly sandbox misconfigurations, instead of taking it as a warning shot.

this is a dangerous narrative btw, exact thinking that will lead to more hf like things.

you can call it a sandbox misconfiguration, sure they are shitty, but do you realize how few people in the world can do what these models did? the entire software ecosystem is full of vulnerabilities and human errors.

like whole sandboxes and software security is largely built around assumptions about what attackers can and can't do, not some formally verified guarantee about what's impossible. it's entirely possible that gpt-7 or even gpt-6 could find ways to bypass firecracker and gvisor, current sota technologies we have today. would you call that another silly sandbox misconfiguration?

"the model did what it was asked to do" is such a silly argument. the goal was to solve the challenge, not hack production servers to get the answers. whether or not it  was explicitly stated(it is), the fact that model has no common sense and reward hacks is pretty concerning.

items.content:
RT @RomanAnin: I spent 15+ years investigating Russian secret services and organized crime. I know people who served with Putin in the KGB and sat in on his deals with St. Petersburg crime bosses. So let me explain the "diesel deal" the way they would — in gangster slang. Because that's the language Putin actually thinks in.

First, the facts.

Putin just raised Russia's 2027 military budget by 27% to a record 17.1 trillion rubles — about $203 billion. Who budgets that kind of money for a war they're about to end?

The FT reported yesterday that Western intelligence has warned the heads of European defense companies that Russia is plotting to assassinate them.

Since September, Tusk, Macron and the intelligence services of Poland, Czechia, Latvia, Belgium, France and Denmark have all warned that Russian hybrid attacks — including drone and missile strikes — will intensify in the coming months.

None of this looks like a country preparing for peace.

Who actually benefits?

🇺🇸 What the US gets: Every serious analysis I've read says the announced volumes won't move American diesel prices. This is a PR move for Trump before the midterms — a story about prices that will "very, very soon" come down once his friend Vladimir's tankers reach US shores, plus the chance to claim he ended another war (I've lost count). The only US "benefit" is Trump's rating.

🇷🇺 What Russia gets: billions of dollars to keep funding its genocidal war against Ukrainians. Sanctions relief. A demonstration of power to the rest of the world. A deeper rift between the US and its European allies. And a real chance to disrupt US weapons and intelligence flowing to Ukraine.

So what is Putin's actual goal?

Trump's disapproval is at record highs and polls show his party will most likely loose midterm elections. In less than a month his power will be badly weakened. Why would Putin sign a long-term peace deal with a lame duck whose signature will soon be scrutinized at best and annulled at worst?

He wouldn't. And here's where the slang comes in.

In the eyes of Putin and his siloviki, Trump is a baryga — a greedy, unscrupulous businessman who puts profit above law and principle. Gangsters despise barygas, but they love using them. The goal is always to turn a baryga into a lokh — a mark, an outsider who doesn't understand the rules of the underworld and gets played to serve the gang's interests.

By signing the diesel deal, Putin plays two scenarios at once:

A) The deal miraculously helps his lokh keep power — great.

B) The deal changes nothing, the baryga loses the midterms — but by then it has already done its job: inflamed US political tensions and acted as arson inside the American system.

Putin knows that the majority of Americans support Ukraine. He knows that by signing, Trump draws unprecedented criticism, including from his own party. And he knows a baryga won't give up power easily, because he will have to answer for everything he did in office — this deal included. That's classic gangster/secret-service method: tie a man to your organization, make him a partner in your crimes, so he can't walk away.

Pouring more oil — diesel, in this case — onto the most explosive fault lines of American politics, raising the stakes for Trump and pushing him past the point of no return serves Putin far better than a peace deal that could be voided within months.

Remember: Putin's goal in the West is chaos, not peace.

items.content:
We identified a malicious npm package, apexacc/cli, which led us to an operation posing as a Web3 accelerator.

Read more about REF8801 by @k33b0i and @DanielStepanic : https://t.co/QPBorc9VJg 

The fake accelerator spent months courting crypto founders with free Claude and Gemini credits.

Our supply-chain monitor caught the package. It was malicious from its first published version.

The 2 Apex packages we examined, and what they deliver:
• apexacc/cli: redirects OpenRouter-labeled model requests to an attacker-controlled API
• apexacc/audit: MCP server whose 18 tools return fabricated findings
• macOS payload: CloudSyncD backdoor
• Windows payload: infostealer that exfiltrates to Telegram

We asked the operation's scoring tool to rate a project that doesn't exist. It scored 51 in every category, and said its AI scorer was down.

RT @0xJohannes_: UPDATE: I can confirm that the Ledger supply chain is compromised in Europe as well. @Ledger should initiate an immediate product recall to protect users.

This indicates its a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe (comprising over 1,000 stores across 11 countries).

My initial hypothesis was that these devices were returns that looked unopened to the employees and were just sold again as new however, a MediaMarkt employee confirmed that the device I purchased was not a return, and that returned Ledgers are sent directly back to the manufacturer rather than resold.

Store records show the inventory originated from Aqipa GmbH. While Ledger's CTO was unsure if Aqipa serves as the direct distributor between Ledger and MediaMarkt, it appears to be the case. Given that Aqipa distributes across Europe, any physical retail store receiving stock through them may be at risk.

I sent the first ledger to mark and the second one is going to ledger now, so that they can analyse it.
If you purchased a ledger from anyone other than the official ledger store, make sure to check your device!!

items.content:
RT @aakashgupta: Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

items.content:
Defense has fundamentally shifted away from an external actor/campaign-centric model toward insider threat, but so much of what we’ve built over the past 15+ years wasn’t designed for this. Years of ATT&CK bingo have atrophied the muscles required to combat subtle acts of subversion, and now they’re occurring at machine speed and often without the users’ knowledge.

Countless teams I talk with are drowning in alerts generated by agents operating in massive grey areas, doing things that look malicious but are completely benign and vice versa. The missing piece is, as it always has been, the intent behind the action. False positive tuning was already the painful exercise of explaining that intent in org-specific context so we could make exceptions for acceptable behavior. Agents make that substantially harder through their speed, volume, and contextual ambiguity.

The next generation of security controls has to reason about intent in organizational context, because the behaviors we’ve spent many years learning to detect are becoming indistinguishable from the work we’re paying agents to do.
